questions.q: What is a Git branch actually, under the hood?
options: A lightweight, movable pointer to a specific commit, which moves forward as new commits are added
A full copy of every file in the project, duplicated on disk
A separate remote server for that line of work
A permanently frozen snapshot that can never change
questions.explain: Branches are cheap precisely because they're just pointers, not copies of the repository's files.

Creates a new branch called feature-login and switches to it, in one step
Copies all files into a folder named feature-login
Merges feature-login into main
questions.explain: The -c flag tells switch to create the branch first, then check it out — equivalent to the older git checkout -b.

questions.q: While a new branch is checked out and you make commits, what happens to `main`?
options: main is automatically deleted
main merges itself with the new branch instantly
main stays exactly where it was — only the checked-out branch's pointer moves forward
main is renamed to match the new branch
questions.explain: Only the currently checked-out branch's pointer advances with new commits; other branches are untouched until you explicitly merge.

questions.q: In GitHub's web interface, what happens if you type a branch name that doesn't exist yet into the branch selector dropdown?
options: GitHub shows an error and refuses to continue
It silently renames the current branch
Nothing — branches can only be created from the command line
GitHub offers an option to create that branch on the spot, the web equivalent of git switch -c
questions.explain: The branch dropdown on GitHub mirrors local branch creation, offering "Create branch: <name>" when you type a new name.

questions.q: What does `git branch -d old-branch` require in order to succeed?
options: Nothing — it force-deletes regardless of state
That old-branch's changes have already been merged, since -d is the safe delete
That you are currently on the main branch
That the branch has never had any commits
questions.explain: git branch -d is the safe delete — it refuses to delete a branch whose commits haven't been merged elsewhere, to avoid losing work.
